items.title: Bounded-error model comparison: a derivative lower bound confines compatible parameters
items.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\theta_0\in I$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Assume $f(\theta_0)=0$ and that $f'(\theta)\ge m>0$ for every $\theta\in I$. Let a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\hat y|\le s$ with $s\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity. If a model requires $y=f(\theta)$ for some $\theta\in I$, then every $\theta\in I$ compatible with those two simultaneous bounds satisfies $$|\theta-\theta_0|\le\frac{s+\delta}{m};$$ equivalently, if a proposed $\theta$ violates this bound, then the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about the historical reports of the causal-response page.
items.strategy: The triangle inequality for the absolute value ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[def-abs-value]]) gives $|y|\le|\hat y|+|y-\hat y|\le s+\delta$. For $\theta\ne\theta_0$ apply the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) to $f$ on the closed interval with endpoints $\theta$ and $\theta_0$ (an interval contained in $I$ by order convexity, [[def-interval]]): there is $\xi$ strictly between them with $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)=f'(\xi)(\theta-\theta_0)$, hence $|f(\theta)|\ge m|\theta-\theta_0|$ because $f(\theta_0)=0$ and $f'\ge m>0$. Combining $|f(\theta)|=|y|\le s+\delta$ with the lower bound and dividing by $m>0$ gives the stated bound; $\theta=\theta_0$ is immediate. Differentiability of $f$ everywhere and continuity of $f'$ on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]) are used to make $f$ continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on its interior, exactly the mean-value hypotheses.

items.title: Legendre polynomials from a convergent zonal kernel: generating function and exterior expansion
items.statement: For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with $$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$ where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $r>|y|$ with $n=x/|x|$ and $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $\bigl|\,|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\bigr|\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1}$, uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, by analyticity of the kernel in the parameter $y$ ([[def-complex-domain]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]], [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]). This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.
items.strategy: Realness and the degree bound follow by expanding the finite power and integrating the odd cosine moments away; $|P_l(z)|\le1$ uses $|z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta|\le1$. For the generating function integrate the geometric series $\sum_{l\ge0}[q(z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta)]^l=(1-qz-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta)^{-1}$ termwise over $\theta$; the geometric ratio has modulus $\le|q|<1$ uniformly in $\theta$, so the Weierstrass $M$-test gives uniform convergence and termwise integration gives the coefficient representation $P_l$. The integral $\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ for $a>|b|$ is computed by the tangent substitution $u=\tan(\theta/2)$ ([[thm-substitution]], [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]). Substituting $a=1-qz$, $b=-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}$ gives $\pi(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}$. Both sides are holomorphic in $(q,z)$ near the real values with $|q|<1$, where $1-2qz+q^2$ never vanishes, so the identity extends by the identity theorem for holomorphic functions ([[def-complex-domain]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]). Substituting $q=|y|/r$, $z=n\cdot y/|y|$ and using $|P_l|\le1$ gives the geometric tail bound for the displayed kernel expansion. For derivative convergence on a compact observation set, the kernel is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of the parameter domain bounded away from its zeros; Cauchy-type uniform bounds on a slightly larger complex disk ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]) bound every fixed spatial derivative of the series terms by a polynomial in $l$ times $(a/r)^l$, and the ratio test gives uniform convergence of each derivative series. No asymptotic large-$l$ formula is used.

items.title: Global existence, uniqueness and differentiability of the retarded root
items.statement: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.
items.strategy: The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\ge s$, $s\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction.

items.title: Dispersion relations for an absolutely continuous integrable causal kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let $$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$ be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$ The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.
items.strategy:
Treat each real entry $k=K_{jk}$ separately. Its locally absolutely continuous representative is the one in the statement; the published [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] applies on $[0,N]$ under the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice and yields $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^s k\prime(u)du$. Since $k\prime\in L^1$, dominated convergence shows this has a finite limit $\ell=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k\prime$. If $\ell\ne0$, then $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all sufficiently large $s$, contradicting $k\in L^1$ by monotonicity of the integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence $k(s)\to0$.
The defining integral is bounded by $\|k\|_1$ on $\overline H$, and dominated convergence gives joint continuity there ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Writing $z=x+iy$, the real parameter derivatives of $k(s)e^{izs}$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$. On any rectangle in $H$ their absolute values are bounded by $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied separately in $x,y$ supplies the partials; dominated convergence makes them continuous, and $\partial_y\chi=i\partial_x\chi$ gives holomorphy by [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\chi\prime(\omega)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{i\omega s}ds$.
For fixed $z\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get
$$\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^N k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$
This is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem. For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, $|e^{izs}|\le1$; $k(N)\to0$ kills the endpoint term and dominated convergence applies to both integrals. Thus
$$\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac1{iz}\int_0^\infty k\prime(s)e^{izs}ds,\qquad |\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k\prime\|_1}{|z|}.$$
For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $F$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $F(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $F$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $F(z+i\delta)\to F(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $F(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi F(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[F(\xi)-F(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi F(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply the preceding step to each entry of $\chi$. Adding the stipulated real instantaneous matrix means the total transfer function is $\chi_\infty+\chi$; subtract $\chi_\infty$ before taking the principal values. All scalar claims are the $d=1$ case. Neither temporal causality nor these analytic identities impose the separate passivity quadratic-form condition.

items.title: Poincare inequality with mean subtraction on a bounded connected C-one domain
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice (used through the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem below) and the Axiom of Countable Choice (declared by the flattening and Sobolev suppliers). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain in the graph sense ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-connected-space]]); its closure is compact, so the boundary has a finite cover by boundary charts ([[def-compact-space]]). There is a constant $C_\Omega$, depending only on $\Omega$, with $$\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad v_\Omega:=\frac1{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega v\,dx .$$ Here $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the weak coordinate derivatives, and $\nabla v$ denotes the weak gradient. The estimate is the mean-zero (Poincare) inequality needed for weak Neumann solvability, where the mean-zero subspace carries the gradient norm.
items.strategy:
On a rectangular box $R$ the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along coordinate segments with Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $\int_R\int_R|v(x)-v(y)|^2dx\,dy\le C_R|R|\int_R|
abla v|^2dx$; replacing $x$ by $y$ one coordinate at a time bounds the squared finite sum by three times the sum of the three one-coordinate differences, and Fubini-Tonelli ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) integrates the remaining coordinates. Jensen's inequality ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality]]) against the normalised $y$-integral gives the local mean estimate $\int_R|v-v_R|^2\le C'_R\int_R|
abla v|^2$. The same argument applies to a half-box. Each boundary graph chart is flattened to a half-box; the $C^k$ boundary flattening lemma ([[lem-c-k-boundary-flattening-preserves-wkp-locally]]) transports the estimate to the chart patch, initially for smooth functions and then for $H^1$ functions by the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem ([[thm-smooth-up-to-the-boundary-density-on-smooth-domains]]), with bounded chart Jacobians and first derivatives. Interior balls are replaced by boxes contained in $\Omega$. Compactness of the boundary and of the residual interior region gives a finite connected cover $\Omega= igcup_jU_j$ with every $|U_j|>0$ and a connected intersection graph: otherwise the finite disjoint unions of graph components would be nonempty relatively open sets partitioning the connected $\Omega$ ([[def-connected-space]]). Writing $a_j$ for the mean of $v$ on $U_j$, the local estimates give $\|v-a_j\|_{L^2(U_j)}\le C_j\|
abla v\|_{L^2(U_j)}$, and the mean differences $|a_j-a_k|$ over nonempty overlaps are bounded by the local gradient energy along a finite spanning tree of the intersection graph. Summing the local squared bounds and the squared mean differences over the finite cover, and using that the global mean minimises $a\mapsto\int_\Omega|v-a|^2$, gives the stated bound.

items.title: Outgoing spherical radial functions: exact bounds on the spherical Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient
items.statement: For $l\in\mathbb N_0$ and $z>0$ set $$h_l(z)=(-i)^{l+1}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\sum_{j=0}^{l}\frac{i^j\,(l+j)!}{j!\,(l-j)!\,(2z)^j}.$$ Then $h_l$ is a complex-valued $C^2$ function of $z>0$ solving $$h_l''(z)+\frac2z h_l'(z)+\Bigl[1-\frac{l(l+1)}{z^2}\Bigr]h_l(z)=0,$$ it never vanishes on $(0,\infty)$, and its Wronskian-type identity $\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_l(z)}\,h_l'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}$ holds. For $k>0$ and $R>0$ the spherical Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient $$t_l=\frac{k\,h_l'(kR)}{h_l(kR)}$$ satisfies the exact bounds $$\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-\frac1R,\qquad |\operatorname{Re}t_l|\le\frac{l+1}{R},\qquad 0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k .$$ These are exact identities and inequalities for the displayed explicit functions, not asymptotic formulas; the argument uses only elementary differentiation and a constant Wronskian, so no large-$l$ asymptotic input is required.
items.strategy: Substituting $h=e^{iz}P(z)/z$ with $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^l b_jz^{-j}$ into the radial equation gives the coefficient recursion $b_{j+1}=i(l+j+1)(l-j)b_j/[2(j+1)]$ with $b_0=1$, terminating at $j=l$ because $l-j=0$; its solution is the displayed factorial formula, which proves the equation and shows the leading outgoing term $(-i)^{l+1}e^{iz}/z$ with a finite remainder. Writing $y=zh_l$ gives $y''+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})y=0$ with real coefficient; differentiating $\operatorname{Im}(\overline y\,y')$ and using the equation shows its derivative is zero, so by the zero-derivative-implies-constant corollary on the interval $(0,\infty)$ ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]) it is constant, and its large-$z$ leading exponential gives the constant $1$: hence $\operatorname{Im}(\overline{h_l}h_l')=z^{-2}\ne0$, so $h_l$ never vanishes. For the real bounds set $F=|y|^2=|P|^2$; since $b_j$ carries phase $i^j$ times a real number, odd cross terms cancel and $F$ is an even finite polynomial in $z^{-1}$, $F=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jz^{-2j}$ with $a_0=1$. Differentiating the real equation gives $F'''+4(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})F'+4l(l+1)Fz^{-3}=0$, whose coefficient matching yields $a_{j+1}=(2j+1)[l(l+1)-j(j+1)]a_j/[2(j+1)]$, all positive for $0\le j\le l$ and zero at $j=l+1$, with the closed form $a_j=(2j)!(l+j)!/[2^{2j}(j!)^2(l-j)!]$. Thus $|h_l|^2=z^{-2}\sum a_jz^{-2j}\ge z^{-2}$ and half the logarithmic derivative gives $\operatorname{Re}[kh_l'/h_l]=-R^{-1}\bigl[\sum_ja_j(kR)^{-2j}+\sum_j j a_j(kR)^{-2j}\bigr]/\sum_ja_j(kR)^{-2j}$, a weighted average of $j\in\{0,\dots,l\}$, so it lies in $[-\,(l+1)/R,\,-1/R]$. The Wronskian identity gives $\operatorname{Im}[kh_l'(kR)/h_l(kR)]=k/(k^2R^2\,|h_l(kR)|^2)=k/(k^2R^2|h_l|^2)\in(0,k]$ using $|h_l|^2\ge z^{-2}$. The derivative computations use the algebra of derivatives and the entireness of the complex exponential ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]).

items.title: Rectangular PEC reflection class: Fourier completeness, weak solutions and energy conservation
items.statement: Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.
items.strategy: The one-dimensional character system on the torus is complete for complex $L^2$ ([[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]) and its Fourier partial sums converge in mean square ([[thm-l-two-fourier-series-converges-in-mean-square]]). If an $L^2(Q)$ function is orthogonal to every product of characters, fix two indices and integrate against those two characters: Fubini and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make the remaining one-variable coefficient an $L^2$ function whose character coefficients all vanish, hence it is zero; repeating in the second and third coordinates on a single null set gives product completeness; orthogonality follows by iterated one-variable integration and Parseval by expanding the squared distance to a finite projection. Reflection parities force sine in odd coordinates and cosine in even coordinates; the trigonometric product modes are the paired $\pm k_j$ projections. For each torus wavevector $k_j=\pi n_j/L_j$ the Fourier coefficients satisfy the finite-dimensional constant-coefficient linear system $\widehat E_t=i(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}k\times\widehat B$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$ with $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$. The system is Lipschitz, so the maximal-solution theorem ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]) gives a unique solution through the initial coefficients, and differentiating $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+|\widehat B|^2/\mu$ gives zero by the scalar triple-product identity and conjugation, so its weighted norm is preserved and the solution is global; the constrained subspace and the parity patterns are preserved because $k\cdot(k\times v)=0$ and curl maps the stated parities into each other. Solve all coefficients, truncate to finitely many wavevectors, and pass to the limit with Parseval: the weighted tail norm equals its initial value, so the finite solutions converge uniformly in time in $L^2$, and the limit is $C_tL^2$ and satisfies the equations in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]]) after testing against smooth periodic compactly supported-in-time tests, whose coefficients and derivatives are summable. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous Fourier coefficients whose distributional derivatives are the displayed continuous right-hand sides; testing the difference of two solutions against smooth periodic tests and using the vanishing of the difference's distributional derivative yields equality of the coefficients, and energy conservation passes to the limit in norm.

items.title: Newtonian potential of smooth compact data is smooth and solves the Poisson equation pointwise
items.statement: Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.
items.strategy: Substitute $z=x-y$: $Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)f(x-z)\,dz$ with $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On a compact set of $x$ the derivatives $D^\alpha f(x-z)$ vanish outside a common bounded $z$-set and are bounded there, so every parameter derivative has an integrable bound $C|\Phi|$ on that set; differentiation under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], applied coordinatewise) gives $D^\alpha Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x-z)\,dz$ and continuity of the result, hence $C^\infty$. The distributional identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ is the cited Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]). Since both sides are smooth functions (the right side is $f$, the left side is a smooth representative by the first part), the distributional equality is a pointwise equality by localization against compactly supported nonnegative smooth tests. The derivative identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$ is the parameter-differentiation formula just proved, and the final smoothness claim for $E$ follows by linearity.

items.title: Unique solution of a symmetric coercive variational problem on a Hilbert space
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, or the Axiom of Choice as declared ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]), let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bounded bilinear form ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]) with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for all $v\in H$ and some $\alpha>0$, and let $\ell:H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional with dual norm $\|\ell\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then there is exactly one $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$. No Lax-Milgram theorem, Zorn-type argument or unproved minimiser existence is invoked: the proof minimises the explicit functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$.
items.strategy: The functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$ is bounded below by $\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\|v\|$ and tends to $+\infty$ as $\|v\|\to\infty$. Choose a minimising sequence $v_n$ with $J(v_n)\to m=\inf J$; the choice of the sequence uses Countable Choice as declared ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The parallelogram law ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]) gives $J((v_n+v_k)/2)=[J(v_n)+J(v_k)]/2-a(v_n-v_k,v_n-v_k)/8$, so $\alpha\|v_n-v_k\|^2/8\le[J(v_n)+J(v_k)]/2-m\to0$: the sequence is Cauchy, and completeness of the Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]) gives $v_n\to u$ in norm, with $J(u)=m$ by continuity of the bounded form and functional ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]). For fixed $v$ the real quadratic $s\mapsto J(u+sv)$ has a minimum at $s=0$, so its linear coefficient $a(u,v)-\ell(v)$ vanishes; conversely any such $u$ satisfies $J(u+v)-J(u)=\tfrac12a(v,v)\ge0$. Uniqueness: for two solutions test the difference with itself to get $\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|^2\le0$. Testing the equation at $v=u$ gives $\alpha\|u\|^2\le\|\ell\|\|u\|$, hence the estimate.

items.title: Thin closed current: divergence-free distribution and convergence of its mollified Biot-Savart fields
items.statement: Let $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length and let $I\in\mathbb R$ be a constant. Define the vector-valued distribution $$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)\ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) .$$ Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). For a nonnegative smooth radial mollifier $\eta_\varepsilon$ of integral one supported in $B_\varepsilon$ the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon=j*\eta_\varepsilon$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on any compact $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to $$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds .$$ For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/[2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}]$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.
items.strategy: The divergence pairing is $-I\int_0^L\frac{d}{ds}[\psi(\gamma(s))]\,ds=0$ by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) and periodicity ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Mollification commutes with derivatives by compact integration by parts against the test function, so $\operatorname{div}j_\varepsilon=0$ and $j_\varepsilon$ is smooth and compactly supported. If $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,\gamma)>0$ and $\varepsilon<d/2$, the Biot-Savart kernel and each of its finitely many $x$-derivatives are smooth on the compact difference set $(x,y)\in K\times\gamma$ and hence uniformly continuous there ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]); subtracting the mollified and unmollified integrals leaves $|I|L$ times that uniform modulus of continuity at $\varepsilon$ times $\mu_0/(4\pi)$, which tends to zero. For the axis computation the tangential numerator integrates to $2\pi a^2e_z$ and the denominator is $(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}$; the differentiation with respect to the observation point and the parameters is justified by differentiation under the integral sign on the compact set $K$ ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]).

items.title: The gradient norm dominates the H-one norm on zero-boundary Sobolev space
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice as declared by the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, and write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $H_0^1(\Omega):=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)$ the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then $H^1(\Omega)$ and its closed subspace $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are complete, the quadratic integral norm is a Hilbert norm (its coordinate $L^2$ inner products satisfy the parallelogram law), and $$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega). $$ In particular the gradient seminorm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on $H_0^1$, and the argument needs neither a smooth domain nor a general boundary-trace theorem.
items.strategy: For $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ extend $v$ by zero to the box $(-L,L)^3$ (legitimate because $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$). Along each coordinate line the Newton-Leibniz formula ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]) gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-L}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$; Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $|v|^2\le2L\int_{-L}^{L}|\partial_1v|^2ds$, and integrating in the other coordinates and then in $x_1$ over a length-$2L$ interval gives $\|v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2$, hence the displayed squared inequality with $(2L)^2$ and the nonsquared bound $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2$. Approximation in the $W^{1,2}$ norm (the definition of $H_0^1$ as a closure, [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) passes both the inequality and the equivalences to all of $H_0^1$ by continuity of the $L^2$ norm; completeness is the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]) restricted to the closed subspace, and the Hilbert-norm claim follows because the $W^{1,2}$ quadratic norm is induced by the coordinate $L^2$ inner products, which satisfy the parallelogram law.

items.title: The L-two Dirichlet resolvent and smooth zero-boundary test density
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let `Omega` be a bounded `C∞` domain in `R3`, in the graph sense of `def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts`; connectedness is unnecessary. Write `H^m(Omega)=W^{m,2}(Omega;R)` with the multi-index integral norm and `H0^1(Omega)` for the `H1` closure of `Cc∞(Omega)`. For every real `f in L2(Omega)` there is a unique `u in H0^1(Omega) ∩ H2(Omega)` satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies `(1−Delta)u=f` distributionally and almost everywhere as an `L2` identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover `D={phi in C∞(closure Omega): phi|boundary Omega=0}` is dense in `H2(Omega) ∩ H0^1(Omega)` in the `H2` norm: every such `w` has `phi_j in D` with `phi_j→w` in `H2`. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function in a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular, `grad phi_j→grad w` in the graph norm of `H(curl) ∩ H(div)`, with zero curl and `div grad w=Delta w`; every `grad phi_j` is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let `X_Omega` be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with `nu cross v=0` on the boundary, where `nu` is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real `L2` vector fields whose distributional `div v=sum_i partial_i v_i` and `curl v=(partial_2 v_3-partial_3 v_2, partial_3 v_1-partial_1 v_3, partial_1 v_2-partial_2 v_1)` lie in `L2`; its norm squared is `||v||2^2+||curl v||2^2+||div v||2^2`. Thus `grad w` belongs to this explicitly defined `X_Omega`, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of `f`, no classical boundary value for general `u`, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in `H0^1`; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.
items.strategy:
1. **Variational existence and its sharp H1 bound.** B1 supplies completeness and the Hilbert structure of `H0^1`. Equip it with the full quadratic `H1` norm and set `a(w,v)=integral(grad w·grad v+wv)`. Cauchy–Schwarz on the four-component `L2` tuple makes this a bounded symmetric form, and `a(v,v)=||v||H1²`, so the coercivity constant is exactly one. The functional `ell(v)=integral fv` has norm at most `||f||2` because `||v||2≤||v||H1`. Apply B2's explicit minimizing-sequence solver, with its declared Countable Choice covered by AC, to obtain the unique weak `H0^1` solution and `||u||H1≤||f||2`. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions gives the distributional equation. No Lax–Milgram result or unproved minimizer theorem is substituted. None of B1's numerical Poincaré constants is used.

2. **Charts and admissible tangential tests.** Cover the compact closure by finitely many interior patches and smooth graph patches. Shrink each patch twice, with compact support away from its artificial sides, and choose cutoffs equal to one on the inner patches. A graph flattening followed, if needed, by reversal of the last coordinate sends the domain side to `t>0`; smooth charts and inverse bounds through order two give bounded local `H1` and `H2` changes of variables. With `y=Phi(x)`, `J=|det D(Phi^{-1})|`, `U=u∘Phi^{-1}`, the local weak equation is

$$\int A_{ij}\partial_jU\partial_iV+cUV=\int FV,\qquad A=J(D\Phi)(D\Phi)^{\mathsf T},\quad c=J,\quad F=J(f\circ\Phi^{-1}).$$

All coefficients and first derivatives are bounded on the chosen patch, `A` is symmetric and uniformly positive, and `||F||2≤C||f||2` locally. The change-of-variables formula and weak chain rule justify these identities. A localized flattened `U` lies in `H0^1` of the half-space: take the sequence of `Cc∞(Omega)` functions defining the original `H0^1` membership, multiply by the patch cutoff, and pull back. These are smooth compactly supported functions on the open half-space and converge in `H1`; their supports need not have a uniform distance from its boundary. Hence tangential translations and smooth cutoffs preserve this closure. For `k=1,2`, `w_h=delta_h^k U` and `V=−delta_{−h}^k(eta² w_h)` are admissible tests, pulled back and extended by zero outside the chart. Use a larger preliminary localization equal to one on the quotient neighbourhood, so its cutoff never changes the original equation on the test support. Interior patches allow all three quotient directions. No normal quotient crosses the boundary.

3. **The L2-data estimate, with no differentiated datum.** Put `S=F−cU`, only in `L2`. Discrete integration by parts and the quotient product rule give the principal term

$$\int\eta^2 A_{ij}(y+he_k)\partial_jw_h\partial_iw_h\ge\alpha\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2^2.$$

The exact remaining principal terms are `integral eta²(delta_h Aij)∂jU ∂iw_h` and `integral [Aij(y+h)∂jw_h+(delta_h Aij)∂jU](∂i eta²) w_h`. Thus their absolute sum is at most

$$C\bigl(\|U\|_{H^1}+\|w_h\|_2\bigr)\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+C\|U\|_{H^1}\|w_h\|_2.$$

Here `||delta_h A||infinity≤||∂k A||infinity`, and the published directional increment estimate yields `||w_h||2≤C||U||H1` on the required enlarged quotient neighbourhood. The undifferentiated right side obeys

$$\left|\int S\,\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2w_h)\right|\le C\|S\|_2\bigl(\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+\|w_h\|_2\bigr),$$

because the same increment bound applies to `eta²w_h` in that direction. Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality absorb half the principal gradient square and give, uniformly for all sufficiently small nonzero `h`,

$$\|\eta\nabla\delta_h^kU\|_2\le C(\|F\|_2+\|U\|_{H^1}).$$

This estimates the actual `L2` datum, not its difference quotient; no `delta_h F` or derivative of `f` is present. The published tangential-test lemma supplies the exact commutator identity, but this explicit estimate is still part of the new proof.

4. **Weak mixed derivatives and corrected normal recovery.** On a smaller patch where `eta=1`, for every compactly supported smooth test `psi`, discrete integration by parts gives `integral delta_h^k(∂jU) psi = −integral ∂jU delta_{−h}^k psi`, whose limit is `−integral ∂jU ∂k psi`. The uniform bound in step 3 makes this distribution a bounded functional in the `L2` norm on tests. Extend it continuously to the closed `L2` subspace generated by those tests, which is Hilbert by `L2` completeness; Riesz gives an `L2` representing function with the same bound. This represents `∂k∂j U` distributionally. No weakly convergent subsequence, reflexivity theorem, or asserted density of tests in the whole `L2` space is required. Thus boundary patches have every second derivative with at least one tangential index; weak derivatives commute by testing smooth functions. The divergence-form equation gives the missing normal derivative with the signs

$$A_{33}\partial_{33}U=cU-F-\sum_{(i,j)\ne(3,3)}A_{ij}\partial_{ij}U-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_iA_{ij})\partial_jU.$$

Every term on the right is in `L2` and `A33≥alpha>0`, so division yields `∂33U in L2` and its bound. This follows distributionally before making the almost-everywhere identification. Interior patches already have all second derivatives. Return through the bounded `H2` chart maps, sum the finitely many inner-patch estimates, and obtain `||u||H2≤C(||f||2+||u||H1)≤C_Omega||f||2`. The equation now holds in `L2`. Uniqueness in `H0^1∩H2` is already uniqueness in the larger variational space.

5. **Zero-trace H2 density: prerequisites and flat gluing.** This step applies to every `w in H2∩H0^1`, not just the resolvent. Use a finite smooth ambient partition with one interior part and boundary parts compactly contained in graph charts. Multiplication and flattening preserve `H2`; a boundary part gives a compactly supported `W in H2(H)` with flat trace zero by chart compatibility and bounded trace continuity (or by the `H0^1` approximating sequence from step 2). Its support is separated from the chart's artificial edges. To justify the reflection, first obtain unrestricted smooth `H2` approximants of `W` on the half-space from the published `k=2,p=2` half-space extension, multiplication by a fixed compact cutoff equal to one on its support, and whole-space mollification. They converge in `H2`, so traces of the functions and their first derivatives converge in `L2` by the published `H1` flat trace bound. For any `zeta in Cc∞(R2)` and tangential `k`, their classical boundary integration by parts gives `integral T(∂kW) zeta = −integral TW ∂k zeta = 0`. Hence `T(∂kW)=0` as a distribution and almost everywhere; uniqueness of regular distributions follows directly from mollification/test pairings. This proves the needed tangential trace identity, rather than assuming it.

Define the odd reflection `W_o(y,t)=W(y,t)` for `t>0`, `−W(y,−t)` for `t<0`. A piecewise `H1` function whose two traces agree is globally `H1`: prove this by testing each half against a compact smooth ambient test, using smooth half-space approximation, one-variable integration and Fubini; the sole interface contribution is the difference of its two traces and hence cancels. Apply this gluing calculation first to `W_o` (both traces zero), then to its first derivatives. The tangential derivatives are odd reflections of `∂kW`, with both traces zero by the preceding argument. The normal derivative is the even reflection of `∂tW`, with identical traces on both sides; its trace need not vanish. Thus `W_o in H2(R3)`, and each derivative has the indicated reflected `L2` class; its `H2` norm is `sqrt(2)||W||H2`. No delta layer occurs. Even reflection of `W`, or zero extension in `H2`, would generally fail and is not used.

6. **Mollification, localization, and the actual cavity norm.** Choose a real compactly supported mass-one mollifier invariant under `t→−t`, for example a radial one, and convolve `W_o`. The mollifications converge in `H2(R3)` because weak derivatives commute with convolution and the `L2` approximate identity converges for each of the finitely many derivatives. They remain odd, so vanish exactly at `t=0`. Multiply by a fixed smooth cutoff in the flattened ambient chart equal to one near the support of `W_o`, with support separated from the artificial edges. This preserves boundary vanishing and convergence. For all sufficiently small radii the cutoff may also be chosen even in `t`, although only zero values at `t=0` are needed after multiplication. Pull back through the smooth chart and extend by zero outside its artificial support to get globally smooth functions on a neighbourhood of the closure with zero physical boundary value. Approximate the interior part by compactly supported smooth functions using legitimate compact-support zero extension and mollification, with radii smaller than its distance from the physical boundary. Add the finitely many parts, choosing radii tending to zero (AC covers sequence choices), to obtain `phi_j→w` in `H2` with `phi_j|boundary=0`. Each lies in `H0^1` by the published zero-trace kernel theorem. Finally `curl grad phi_j=0`, `div grad phi_j=Delta phi_j`, and `n×grad phi_j=0`, the last identity following by differentiating the identically zero smooth boundary restriction. Therefore

$$\|\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w\|_2+\|\operatorname{curl}(\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w)\|_2+\|\operatorname{div}(\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w)\|_2\longrightarrow0.$$

The curls vanish distributionally by commutation of weak derivatives, which is a direct test-function calculation. This is exactly convergence in G3's graph norm, giving `grad w in X` without a maximal-trace-density assumption.

items.title: Dispersion relations for a finitely subtracted analytic response
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$, $$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ $$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$ At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), let $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ be real scalar coefficients or real matrices, and let $K$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^m A_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^m A_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.
items.strategy:
[[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]] on a complex neighborhood of $\omega_0$ shows that $\chi-P$ has a zero of order at least $n$, so division gives the holomorphic removable continuation of $f$ there. Elsewhere in $H$ its denominator is nonzero. Continuity of $\chi$ on $\overline H$ and the removable continuation make $f$ continuous on $\overline H$; its real restriction is $C^1$ by hypothesis. The growth bound on $\chi$ and the degree of $P$ give $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly in $\overline H$ at infinity. For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $f$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $f$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $f(z+i\delta)\to f(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $f(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[f(\xi)-f(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply that boundary-contour argument to $f$, multiply both formulas by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$, and add the complex polynomial $P$. At $\omega_0$ the factor vanishes and the removable Taylor identity gives the asserted Taylor value. The imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex $P$; it cannot be omitted.
For the distinct constitutive branch, multiplication by $(-i\omega)^j$ is the derivative multiplier on the stipulated monochromatic histories, so the transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$. Derivatives at a time are determined by a history agreeing on its whole past, including its endpoint, and the convolution is causal; hence their finite sum is causal on histories with the stated bounded continuous derivatives. The residual $\chi-Q=\chi_K$ satisfies [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]] entrywise. Without that lemma's AC and integrability conditions a merely integrable causal kernel still gives a bounded upper-half-plane holomorphic response, but does not automatically supply these principal values or Taylor continuation. The stated additional analytic assumptions, not causality alone, govern the Taylor branch.

items.title: Weak Dirichlet existence for a prescribed lift and uniformly elliptic coefficient
items.statement:
Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric real $3	imes3$ matrix field on $\Omega$ with $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le eta|\xi|^2$ for a.e. $x$ and all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $0<\alpha\le eta<\infty$, let $G\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a specified lift, and let $F\in(H_0^1(\Omega))^*$ be bounded. Then there is exactly one $u\in G+H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $$\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=F(v)\qquad	ext{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$ where $H_0^1=W_0^{1,2}$ carries the gradient norm. For $F(v)=\int_\Omegaho v$ with $ho\in L^2(\Omega)$ this is the weak Poisson solution $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$, with the homogeneous boundary datum represented by membership of $H_0^1$ rather than by an unproved classical trace. No boundary datum outside the specified lift class is assumed attainable; classical boundary regularity, general Neumann lifts and transmission regularity remain later obligations.
items.strategy:
On $H_0^1$ the gradient norm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm and $H_0^1$ is complete ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]]). Put $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla w$ and $\ell(v)=F(v)-a(G,v)$ for $v,w\in H_0^1$. The coefficient bounds and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make $a$ a bounded symmetric bilinear form with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|
abla v\|_2^2$, and $\ell$ is bounded because $F$ is bounded and $a(G,\cdot)$ is controlled by $ eta\|
abla G\|_2\|
abla\cdot\|_2$. The symmetric coercive variational solver ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]) gives a unique $w$ with $a(w,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v$, and $u=G+w$ solves the stated problem; testing with compactly supported smooth $v$ gives the distributional equation by the weak first-derivative identity. For $F(v)=\intho v$ with $ho\in L^2$, the bound $|F(v)|\le\|ho\|_2\|v\|_2\le2L\|ho\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$ ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) makes $F$ bounded, so the existence conclusion applies. Across finitely many material interfaces the weak equation encodes flux continuity where one-sided classical traces exist, by integration by parts on each side.

items.title: Magnetic dipole expansion with an explicit uniform remainder
items.statement: Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$, $a>0$, and put $m=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then for $r=|x|\ge2a$ the vector potential and magnetic field $$A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ satisfy, uniformly in $n=x/r$, $$A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^3}\Bigr),\qquad B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^4}\Bigr).$$ The constants in the $O$ terms are absolute (the second follows by differentiating the first, not by differentiating an unspecified remainder), and $\|J\|_1=\int|J|$.
items.strategy: Integrating $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i$ over $\mathbb R^3$ and using the vanishing of the integral of a divergence of a compactly supported $C^1$ field ([[lem-integral-of-a-divergence-of-an-l-one-c-one-field-vanishes]]) gives $\int J_i=0$; integrating $\operatorname{div}(y_iy_jJ)=y_jJ_i+y_iJ_j$ gives antisymmetry of $M_{ij}=\int y_jJ_i$, and with the definition of $m$ one has $M_{ij}=-\varepsilon_{ijk}m_k$ and hence $Mx=m\times x$. Writing $|x-y|^{-1}=r^{-1}+(x\cdot y)/r^3+\text{remainder}$ with the second-order Taylor formula ([[cor-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-peano-remainder]], in its quantitative form), the integral remainder is $\int_0^1(1-s)y_jy_k\,\partial_j\partial_k|x-sy|^{-1}ds$, whose Hessian is $O(r^{-3})$ and whose spatial derivative is $O(r^{-4})$ with absolute constants because $|x-sy|\ge r/2$ on the support; the modulus-of-integral bound ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) against $J$ gives the $A$ estimate and its differentiated estimate. Finally the curl computation $\operatorname{curl}(m\times x/r^3)=3x(m\cdot x)/r^5-m/r^3$ follows by component differentiation of the cross product ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), the first term being the Coulomb-dipole expression of the cited remainder lemma ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]).

items.title: Outgoing source Helmholtz field: fundamental solution, Fraunhofer and Fresnel error terms
items.statement: For $k>0$ define $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ off the origin, a locally integrable complex function. Then $$(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$$ distributionally. For a finite complex measure $\alpha$ supported in $B_a(0)$, the field $u=G_k*\alpha$ is smooth outside the support, solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there and is outgoing: for $x=rn$, $r\ge2a$, $$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$ uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. For a planar aperture $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ with observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$, $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, $a+b\ll z$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$ and relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$, hence absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. Aperture data are an explicitly specified scalar source, not asserted to be the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces, and no uniqueness or existence for arbitrary obstacle boundary data is claimed.
items.strategy: For radial $f(r)$ one has $\Delta f=f''+2f'/r$ by direct coordinate differentiation of $\partial_ir=x_i/r$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), and inserting $f=G_k$ gives $(\Delta+k^2)f=0$ for $r>0$. For the distributional identity excise a ball $B_\delta$ inside a compact test integration; the second Green identity ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) on the excised domain cancels the $k^2$ terms and leaves the inner flux, where $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1)$: the derivative-test boundary term is $O(\delta)$ and the leading unit flux multiplies $\psi(0)$, while the local $k^2G_k$ integral is $O(\delta^2)$; the limit is $\delta_0$ with the displayed sign. Off-support smoothness and all derivatives follow from the positive separation of compact observation and source sets, with differentiation under the source integral. For the Fraunhofer error write $R=|rn-y|$ and use the norm expansion of the cited dipole-remainder technique ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]): $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le Ca^2/r$ and $|r/R-1|\le Ca/r$; the exponential difference is bounded by $C r^{-1}(a/r+ka^2/r)$ via $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$, and integrating against the total variation of $\alpha$ with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) gives the displayed error; the outgoing relation follows from $\partial_rR=1+O(a^2/r^2)$ and $R^{-2}=O(r^{-2})$. The Fresnel estimate is the Taylor expansion of the norm with explicit remainder on the compact small-$s$ region $s=|\xi-y|^2/z^2$, using $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$.

items.title: Spherical harmonics: orthogonal decomposition, complete basis and addition theorem
items.statement: Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$. Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds: $$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$ where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity.
items.strategy: For homogeneous $Q$ of degree $l-2j$, Euler's identity $x\cdot\nabla Q=(l-2j)Q$ gives $\Delta(r^{2j}Q)=2j(2l-2j+1)r^{2j-2}Q+r^{2j}\Delta Q$; the ansatz $H=\sum_ja_jr^{2j}\Delta^jP$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_j=-a_{j-1}/[2j(2l-2j+1)]$ cancels consecutive coefficients in $\Delta H$, and the final $\Delta^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor+1}P$ vanishes by degree, so $H$ is harmonic and $P-H$ is divisible by $r^2$; recursion gives the decomposition. For homogeneous harmonic $H_l,H_m$ the Green identity on the ball ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) gives $0=\int_{S^2}(H_l\partial_nH_m-H_m\partial_nH_l)=(m-l)\int_{S^2}H_lH_m$, whence orthogonality of distinct degrees; if a harmonic of degree $l$ equalled $r^2Q$, its orthogonality to all lower-degree harmonics would force $\int_{S^2}H_l^2=0$, so $H_l=0$; the monomial count $\dim P_l=(l+1)(l+2)/2$ gives $\dim H_l=2l+1$, and restriction is injective by the same homogeneity argument. For density, continuous functions are dense in $L^2(S^2)$ by a finite smooth graph atlas with subordinate smooth cutoffs, pulling each localised function back, mollifying and using the $L^2$ translation and approximate-identity interfaces ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]); the restricted real polynomial algebra is unital and separates points, so Stone-Weierstrass ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general]]) makes it uniformly dense in $C(S^2)$, and the homogeneous-degree decomposition puts every restriction in the finite span of spherical harmonics, giving $L^2$ density. Finite Gram-Schmidt ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]) applied to a fixed ordered monomial elimination basis of each $H_l$ produces the orthonormal bases without an undefined basis selection. For the addition theorem, $K_l(n,n')=\sum_mY_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')$ is independent of the orthonormal basis and rotation-invariant, and for fixed $n'$ it is the unique (up to scale) rotation-invariant homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$, which is the coefficient $|y|^lP_l(n'\cdot y/|y|)$ of the convergent kernel of the zonal lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]); evaluating the diagonal by integrating $K_l(n,n)$ gives $(2l+1)/(4\pi)$, completing the addition theorem.

items.title: The spherical mean identity behind the wave equation
items.statement: Let $c>0$, let $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ (unbounded $f$ is allowed), and define the spherical mean $$M_rf(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n),\qquad r\ge0,$$ with the outward sphere measure of total area $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then $r\mapsto M_rf(x)$ is smooth for $r\ge0$ and satisfies the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity $$\partial_r^2M_rf(x)+\frac2r\partial_rM_rf(x)=\Delta M_rf(x)\qquad(r>0),$$ and the function $H_f(x,t)=t\,M_{ct}f(x)$, $t\ge0$, satisfies $$\partial_t^2H_f=c^2\Delta H_f,\qquad H_f(x,0)=0,\qquad \partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x).$$ All identities are local and need no decay of $f$, since every integration set is compact. This is the pure spherical-mean identity; it makes no claim about finite-domain boundary data or about general rough data.
items.strategy:
Differentiating the compact sphere integral in the parameter $r$ is justified by the parameter-integral lemma ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]], including its surface-measure form). One gets $\partial_rM_rf(x)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{S^2}n\cdot
abla f(x+rn)\,d\Omega$, and the divergence theorem on $B_r(x)$ ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], applied to the $C^1$ field $
abla f$ and using the Euclidean Laplacian, [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) gives $4\pi r^2\partial_rM_rf(x)=\int_{B_r(x)}\Delta f(y)\,dy$. Differentiating this last integral in $r$ (radial derivative of a ball integral; one-variable fundamental theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]]) gives $\partial_r(r^2\partial_rM_rf)=r^2M_r(\Delta f)=r^2\Delta M_rf$, where the second equality uses linearity and the parameter statement to move $\Delta$ through the mean; dividing by $r^2$ gives the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity. Twice differentiating $H_f(x,t)=tM_{ct}f(x)$ with the algebra of derivatives and the chain rule factor $c$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives $\partial_t^2H_f=2c\partial_rM+c^2t\partial_r^2M=c^2t\Delta M=c^2\Delta H_f$ for $t>0$, using the identity just proved; at $t=0$ one has $M_0f=f$ and $\partial_rM_0f=(4\pi)^{-1}
abla f\cdot\int_{S^2}n\,d\Omega=0$ by reflection symmetry, so $H_f(x,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x)$; the defining compact integral is smooth in signed $r$ as well, so the equation extends to $t=0$.

items.title: Ball Poisson series: interior convergence, boundary data and the Poisson kernel
items.statement: Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with harmonic coefficients $f_{lm}$ in an orthonormal basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]), and for $0\le r<1$ set $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ (the $l=0$ term being the constant value at $r=0$). Then the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic there ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, and $u$ is the unique harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$. For continuous $f$ the same function is $$u(rn)=\int_{S^2}\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}f(n')\,d\Omega(n'),$$ it extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary value $f$, and the kernel is positive of total mass one. This is the stated ball boundary branch; generic smooth-domain classical regularity remains a separate obligation.
items.strategy: The addition theorem of the spherical-harmonic lemma gives $\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)|^2=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]); Cauchy-Schwarz over $m$ and then $l$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) bounds the absolute tail at fixed $r\le r_0<1$ by $\|f\|_2[\sum_{l>N}r_0^{2l}(2l+1)/(4\pi)]^{1/2}\to0$. On a smaller closed ball, apply the interior derivative estimates to each harmonic partial-sum difference on balls of fixed radius inside an intermediate ball ([[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]): every derivative is uniformly bounded by the already vanishing uniform bound on the partial sums, so all derivatives are uniformly Cauchy; the limits identify the derivatives of the limit and $\Delta u=0$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Orthogonal expansion gives $\|u(r\,\cdot)-f\|_2^2=\sum_{l,m}(1-r^l)^2|f_{lm}|^2\to0$ by dominated convergence of the summable bound $4\sum|f_{lm}|^2$. For uniqueness, a smooth harmonic $v$ has radial coefficients solving $v_{lm}''+2r^{-1}v_{lm}'-l(l+1)r^{-2}v_{lm}=0$ by the polar Laplacian and $\Delta_{S^2}Y_{lm}=-l(l+1)Y_{lm}$; the two solutions are $r^l$ and $r^{-l-1}$, and smoothness at the origin excludes the second, so a specified $L^2$ boundary limit fixes the coefficient $f_{lm}$ and completeness gives equality. Summing the zonal addition kernels with weights $r^l$ and applying $(1+2r\partial_r)$ to the generating function of the zonal lemma gives the displayed Poisson kernel; it is positive, and its integral is one because only the normalised constant harmonic survives integration. For continuous $f$ uniform boundary convergence follows by splitting the integral into a small spherical neighbourhood of $n$ (where uniform continuity controls the error) and its complement (whose kernel mass tends to zero uniformly).

items.title: Exact Helmholtz boundary representation with actual traces
items.statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain, $k>0$, $x\in\Omega$, and let $u$ be a smooth solution of $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ on $\Omega$ with $f$ smooth, using the outgoing fundamental solution $G_k$ of the source Helmholtz lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then $$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)\,dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl[G_k(x-y)\,\partial_nu(y)-u(y)\,\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\bigr]\,dS_y,$$ with $n$ the outward normal. For an exterior outgoing solution truncated by a large sphere, the same representation holds with the actual inner boundary traces: the outgoing leading terms of $G_k$ cancel the large-sphere Wronskian integrand at leading order and the remaining compact-observation estimate tends to zero. Consequently the identity requires the consistent actual pair of traces $(u|_{\partial\Omega},\partial_nu|_{\partial\Omega})$; assigning both aperture values $u$ and $\partial_nu$ independently is not a well-posed exact boundary prescription, and an expressly adopted scalar aperture-source model is a separate approximation with its own regime of validity.
items.strategy: Apply the second Green identity ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) on $\Omega\setminus B_\delta(x)$ to $u$ and $G_k$. The $k^2$ terms cancel; the unit-flux inner kernel and the continuous limit of $u$ contribute the $-u(x)$ term from $\int(u\Delta G_k-G_k\Delta u)$, while the volume source contributes $\int G_kf$. Letting $\delta\to0$, the derivative-test inner term is $O(\delta)$ and the flux times $u-u(x)$ tends to zero by continuity, giving the displayed formula with the normalisation and outward-hole sign fixed as in the source lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]). For the exterior case, truncate the outgoing solution by a large sphere and use the outgoing radial decay and Wronskian bound of the spherical Hankel lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]): the large-sphere boundary integrand cancels at leading order, and the remaining term at a fixed observation point is $O(R^{-2})\cdot O(R^2)$-free compact estimate tending to zero, so the same representation uses the actual inner traces.

items.title: Fixed-endpoint variation of the relativistic particle functional
items.statement: Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) with $c>0$ the model's conversion constant, let $[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, let $X:[a,b]\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), and let $A_\mu$ be a $C^2$ covector field on a neighbourhood of the image of $X$. For fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations $h:[a,b]\to V$ with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ and for $m,c>0$ and real $q$ consider $$S[X]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds .$$ Then for each such $h$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and stationarity of $S$ under all such variations is equivalent to $$m\frac{dU_\nu}{d\tau}=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu,\qquad \frac{d\tau}{ds}=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}}c,\qquad F=dA,$$ where $U$ is the four-velocity and $\tau$ the proper-time parameter supplied by the observer-decomposition theorem ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). This is a calculation about the chosen functional; adopting it as a physical particle action is an additional model assumption, and it makes no existence claim for coupled singular particles and fields.
items.strategy:
On the compact interval the strict inequalities of future timelikeness have positive margins, so $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for small $|\varepsilon|$ and the integrand is smooth on a compact parameter set; differentiation in $\varepsilon$ under the integral sign is justified by compactness. The free variation gives $\int mc\,\eta(\dot X,\dot h)/\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds=\int mU_
u\dot h^
u ds=-\int m(dU_
u/ds)h^
u ds$ after integration by parts, with the endpoint terms vanishing by $h(a)=h(b)=0$. The coupling variation is $q\int[(\partial_
u A_\mu)h^
u\dot X^\mu+A_
u\dot h^
u]ds=q\int(\partial_
u A_\mu-\partial_\mu A_
u)\dot X^\mu h^
u ds$ with the endpoint terms again zero, i.e. $q\int F_{
u\mu}\dot X^\mu h^
u ds$ for $F=dA$. Thus $\delta S=\int[-m\,dU_
u/ds+qF_{
u\mu}\dot X^\mu]h^
u ds$, and the fundamental variation lemma applied componentwise ([[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]]) makes every coefficient vanish (and conversely). Dividing by the strictly positive $d	au/ds$ obtained from the observer-decomposition theorem ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) gives the stated equation; raising the index gives the tensor form. All objects are the affine-Minkowski ones of the SR supplier ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

items.title: Weak Dirichlet problem with prescribed fractional Sobolev boundary data
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the trace and Sobolev suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic coefficient as in the lift lemma ([[lem-em-lift-specified-dirichlet-existence]]), let $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and prescribe $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$, the fractional Sobolev space of the boundary definition, defined by a finite graph atlas and partition with norm given by the finite sums of localised $L^2$ norms and Gagliardo seminorms ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). Then there is exactly one $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with trace $Tu=g$ solving $$\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\int_\Omega\rho\,v\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$ and the solution depends continuously on $(\rho,g)$: $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|\rho\|_{L^2}+\|g\|_{H^{1/2}})$. The prescribed trace is exact and no classical $C^2$ boundary regularity is inferred.
items.strategy: The sharp trace theorem and its bounded right inverse ([[thm-sharp-trace-theorem-for-w-one-p]], [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]) give a bounded linear $R:H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)\to H^1(\Omega)$ with $TRg=g$; the flat half-space estimates are the normal-line and Hardy estimates exposed in the research argument. The kernel of the trace is $H_0^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]], with the zero-boundary Sobolev space defined as a closure), so $u=Rg+w$ with $w\in H_0^1$; applying the lift lemma with $G=Rg$ ([[lem-em-lift-specified-dirichlet-existence]]) gives the unique $w$ and hence existence, exact trace and uniqueness. Continuous dependence follows from the estimates of the lift and solver lemmas together with the boundedness of $R$: for two data sets, $\|\nabla(w_1-w_2)\|_2\le\alpha^{-1}[2L\|\rho_1-\rho_2\|_2+\beta\|\nabla R(g_1-g_2)\|_2]$, and the $H^1$ estimate follows by adding $\|Rg\|_{H^1}\le C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$.

items.title: Outgoing spherical trace and Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the explicitly used trace and weak Dirichlet-solvability suppliers. Let $k>0$ and $R>0$. Use the sphere-normalised basis $Y^R_{lm}(Rn):=R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ on $S_R$, where $Y_{lm}$ is the complete normalised unit-sphere basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]) and the coefficients $t_l$ of the outgoing radial-function lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]). The map $$T_Rf=\sum_{l,m}t_l\,f_{lm}Y^R_{lm},\qquad f\in H^{1/2}(S_R),$$ is a bounded linear operator $H^{1/2}(S_R)\to H^{-1/2}(S_R)$ with $$\operatorname{Re}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle\le0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle=\sum_{l,m}(\operatorname{Im}t_l)|f_{lm}|^2>0\ \ (f\ne0).$$ It is precisely the outgoing scalar Helmholtz normal derivative at $r=R$: for every $f\in H^{1/2}(S_R)$ the function $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}f_{lm}h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)\,R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ for $r\ge R$ is the unique outgoing finite-local-energy exterior solution with trace $f$ on $S_R$ and normal derivative $T_Rf$ in the weak trace sense; it is smooth away from the sphere, and for smooth $f$ it satisfies the ordinary Sommerfeld condition. No uniform pointwise outgoing condition is asserted for arbitrary rough traces; the outgoing condition there is its modal/weak version. Here finite-local-energy means membership in $H^1(\{R<|x|<R_1\})$ for every finite $R_1>R$, with the $H^{1/2}$ trace on $S_R$; no global $H^1$ or global $L^2$ condition at infinity is imposed. The outgoing modal class consists of the displayed outgoing $h_l$ radial factors with no incoming partners; for rough traces this modal class is the definition, rather than a pointwise Sommerfeld assertion. Here the boundary Sobolev spaces are their complex versions (or complexifications of the real trace spaces), $f_{lm}=\int_{S_R}f\overline{Y^R_{lm}}\,d\sigma_R$, and the DtN dual pairing is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second.
items.strategy: The boundary norm of the fractional Sobolev space is equivalent, for fixed $R$, to $\sum_{l,m}(l+1)|f_{lm}|^2$: for finite harmonic data the harmonic ball extension $\sum_{l,m}(r/R)^lf_{lm}R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ has Dirichlet energy $\sum(l/R)|f_{lm}|^2$ by the first Green identity ([[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) and normal differentiation, and $L^2$ ball norm $\sum R/(2l+3)|f_{lm}|^2$ with the sphere-normalised basis, so its $H^1$ norm is equivalent to $\sum(l+1)|f_{lm}|^2$. For arbitrary $H^{1/2}$ data the bounded right inverse and the weak harmonic Dirichlet solver of the prescribed-data lemma ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]]) give a controlled harmonic $H^1$ extension; the harmonic coefficients and orthogonality of the ball Poisson series lemma ([[lem-em-ball-poisson-series-boundary-convergence]]) show the finite energy partial sums are bounded by its energy, giving both directions of the equivalence. The bounds $|t_l|\le(l+1)/R+k$ of the spherical Hankel lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]) make $T_R$ bounded into the dual weighted space, and the real and imaginary pairings converge with the stated signs, strict positivity following from $\operatorname{Im}t_l>0$ for every $l$. For the exterior realisation, define $u_{lm}(r)=f_{lm}h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)$, $r\ge R$; the finite polynomial positive formula gives $|h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)|\le R/r$ and, by the recurrence, geometric-in-$l$ radial ratios on every compact $r>R$ interval, so the series and all derivatives converge uniformly there, away from the sphere; the smoothness, the weak trace identification and the annular $H^1$ control follow from Green's identity for each mode on $[R,R+\delta]$ and the bounds above. Uniqueness: the general radial Helmholtz solutions are multiples of $h_l(kr)$ and its incoming partner, whose Wronskian is nonzero; Sommerfeld selects $h_l$, and harmonic completeness forces any smooth outgoing exterior solution to have exactly this map. The annular $H^1$ estimates are precisely the finite-local-energy condition; they do not assert global integrability at infinity. At $l=0$, a nonzero outgoing mode is proportional to $e^{ikr}/r$ and its global $L^2$ norm diverges, which confirms why no global energy condition is imposed. Both the ball and exterior radial extensions use $R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ explicitly; the sphere-normalisation is $Y^R_{lm}(Rn)=R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$, giving the stated radial ball-norm factor $R/(2l+3)$ for the sphere-normalised coefficients. For complex boundary data, apply the real prescribed-trace/harmonic solver to the real and imaginary parts and combine; the resulting squared norm is the sum of the two real energy norms, with the stated sesquilinear pairing.

items.title: Weak Neumann and transmission existence with interface charges
items.statement:
